title: Public invited to help Southampton scientists uncover hidden black holes
excerpt: A search is under way to uncover thousands of hidden black holes believed to be lurking in our galaxy
content:
A search is under way to uncover thousands of hidden black holes believed to be lurking in our galaxy.

The University of Southampton has launched the Black Hole Hunters project, inviting amateur astronomers and the public to help identify black holes in the Milky Way using data from NASA’s TESS space telescope.

With only about 70 black holes currently identified in our galaxy, scientists estimate thousands more remain undetected—and citizen scientists could help reveal them.

Dr Adam McMaster from the University of Southampton said: "Black holes are famously elusive and trap light, which hide them from telescopes.

The University of Southampton has launched the Black Hole Hunters project (Image: University of Southampton)

"But they often leave clues because of their strong gravity, which bends light as they orbit around stars creating an effect called gravitational self-lensing.

"Once we detect this, we’ll know an invisible black hole exists."

The project uses an AI system to sift through millions of possible locations, narrowing down the search for volunteers to review.

Participants are asked to examine simple graphs and animations to spot patterns which could indicate the presence of a black hole.

Grace Clarke, a 20-year-old physics and astronomy student at the University of Southampton, said: "There's still so little we know about black holes so the idea of finding one in our backyard is very exciting.

"I can search for black holes on my laptop from my bedroom—and could make a real impact on real space science.

"The data’s easy to understand, it's just pattern recognition, and you don't need a degree in astronomy to read it."

The Southampton team has processed vast amounts of data from TESS, converting it into easy-to-read visual formats for public analysis.

Dr McMaster said: "We now need people to look at these graphs and flag anything that catches their eye.

"It’s a simple task with no expertise required, and we show volunteers examples of what to look for so all they have to do is recognise the right patterns.

"You’ll be narrowing down precisely where we need to point our telescopes next and you might be the one to discover a black hole."

No specialist equipment is needed to take part—just a computer, phone or tablet and an internet connection.
